from-brief-to-wireframe.title: Welcome to From brief to wireframe, part of Web Designing.
from-brief-to-wireframe.idea: Most disappointing websites fail for structural reasons: the enquiry form is three clicks away, the services page never says what the business does, the phone number is buried in a footer, and the page carries four competing calls to action. None of those are visual problems, and none of them are cheap to fix once a site is built. Wireframing is where they are solved, and it requires a pencil, not a design tool.
from-brief-to-wireframe.example: A private school has a website where applications are "down 40%". The existing site has eight top-level menu items, a home page with a slideshow, and an application form four clicks deep under "Admissions → Forms → Download". The head teacher believes the problem is the colours. The brief converts the complaint into an objective: twelve completed enquiries a month, with the source of each recorded. And the audience is not "parents" — it is parents considering a change in the next term, who are comparing three schools and want three specific facts: fees, location, and results. The sitemap drops from eight menu items to four: Admissions, Academics, About, Contact. The fees move to the top of the Admissions page, because hiding them wastes the time of both the school and the parent. The application becomes a two-field enquiry form (name and phone number) instead of a twelve-field form and a PDF: an enquiry is not an application, and asking for everything up front loses the lead. The phone number and WhatsApp link are pinned in the header on mobile, because that is how the parents actually make contact. The wireframe of the home page answers three questions above the fold, with one action. The result after two months: 31 enquiries, 22 traceable to the website, and a click-to-call from the mobile header in 40% of sessions. The colours never changed.
from-brief-to-wireframe.challenge: Take one real client or organisation and produce a complete structure pack: a one-page brief, a content list with owners, a sitemap, two user flows, mobile and desktop wireframes for the three most important pages, and the findings from testing a clickable prototype with five people. Report the structural changes the testing produced, and the one page you decided the site does not need.

visual-design-for-screens.title: Welcome to Visual design for screens, part of Web Designing.
visual-design-for-screens.idea: Web design has two audiences: the visitor, who needs to find and do something in seconds, and the developer, who has to build it. Good visual design serves both by being systematic — a small set of type sizes, colours, spacings and components used consistently — which is faster to produce, easier to maintain and more persuasive than a page of one-off decisions.
visual-design-for-screens.example: A first visual for a services site uses eleven text sizes, seven greys, three button styles and spacing values of 7, 13, 18, 22, 27 and 35 px. It looks fine on the one page it was designed for, and nobody can build a second page that matches it. The repair is to derive a system from the design's intent — the biggest heading, the base text, the accent colour, the button shape — and then express everything as tokens. Note that this is not restriction for its own sake: the six type sizes below carry the same hierarchy the eleven did, better, because the gaps between them are large enough to see. The practical test of a system is the second page: hand the tokens and components to somebody else and ask them to lay out a new page without asking you a question. If they can produce something that looks like the same site, the system works. That is also what makes the handover to a developer cheap, because the tokens map directly onto CSS custom properties.
visual-design-for-screens.challenge: Produce a complete visual design for a real five-page site: tokens, components with states, mobile and desktop layouts for every page, real content with written microcopy, images within the budget, and the empty, loading and error states. Test it on a real phone over a throttled connection, then hand it to a developer and record — without answering in person — what they could not build unambiguously from it.

handover-development-and-seo.title: Welcome to Handover, development and being found, part of Web Designing.
handover-development-and-seo.idea: Designs fail between the design and the build more often than they fail on the page: unlabelled states, images without exports, colours described as "the blue", a mobile layout left to imagination. Everything in this lesson is about making your intent survive translation — and then about the half of findability that you, as the designer, control more than the developer does.
handover-development-and-seo.example: A designer hands over a five-page site. The developer's questions, in the two scenarios, show exactly where the value lies in a handover package. Handover A (files and a message). Where is the mobile version? Which of the two blues is the link colour? What happens when the client's name is longer than the mock-up? Is this heading a heading or just big text? What does the form do when the email is invalid? What format should the logo be? Who writes the meta descriptions? Every question costs a day of delays and produces decisions the designer should have made. Handover B (package). The design file has mobile and desktop frames, labelled states and annotations; a tokens file lists every colour with its hex value and use; the asset folder contains named images at the correct sizes and an SVG logo; the content document has all copy, titles and descriptions; the brief states the goal and the conversions to track. The developer asks two questions in total, both about a hosting detail. The measurable difference: Handover A took eleven days and two rounds of corrections; Handover B shipped in four. The design's quality is identical in both — only the package changed.
handover-development-and-seo.challenge: Deliver one complete website project from design to launch: the handover package, the built site reviewed on a real phone, the deviation log with each difference agreed or fixed, page titles and descriptions written for every page, analytics with two conversions live, and a launch report showing the before-and-after state of the client's objective. Then measure the goal for four weeks and write the honest result.

clients-pricing-and-portfolio.title: Welcome to Clients, pricing and a portfolio that gets work, part of Web Designing.
clients-pricing-and-portfolio.idea: A designer who can produce good work but cannot price it, scope it or explain it will earn less than a mediocre designer who can. The gap is not talent; it is the practices in this lesson, most of which take an hour to set up once and then apply to every project afterwards.
clients-pricing-and-portfolio.example: A restaurant asks for a website. Quote A is the beginner's version, sent as a WhatsApp message; Quote B is a proposal built from the process in this lesson. Quote A produces a negotiation about the number, a client who keeps adding pages, no deposit, and a designer who spends three weekends on a GH₵400 job and then maintains it for free forever because "it is only small changes". The work is not bad; the structure is. Quote B separates the build from the recurring care, states what is included and excluded, requires a deposit, and prices the content work — which is the part the client cannot do. Note the maintenance line: it is small, recurring, defined, and it is what turns a one-off project into a relationship. It also gives the client permission to call you, which prevents the alternative — unpaid ad-hoc requests for years. The two packages differ by about GH₵1,100 up front and GH₵150 a month, and in practice they differ far more in what happens after the invoice: one client disappears, the other refers two more.
clients-pricing-and-portfolio.challenge: Run one complete cycle on a real opportunity: find a local business with a weak or missing website, prepare three specific observations and a mock-up of its home page before contacting them, hold the first conversation without pitching, and send a one-page proposal with a care plan attached. Then write a half-page review: what the conversation taught you that your assumptions had wrong, and which clause of your proposal you will change next time.
